title: Bison manual: The Bison Parser Algorithm
version: Historical GNU manual mirror at MIT, viewed 2026-10-13
why: Primary description of Bison's bottom-up parser algorithm.

claim: Regular expressions and finite-state recognizers cannot recognize arbitrarily balanced parentheses.
quote: The inability to match brackets, be they ( ), { }, or begin and end is a fundamental limitation of REs; the corresponding recognizers cannot count because they have only a finite set of states.

locator: Section 3.2.2, printed p. 90, PDF p. 117, definition of S
claim: A CFG designates a nonterminal as its start symbol, representing its sentences.
quote: is a nonterminal symbol designated as the start symbol or goal symbol of the grammar. S represents the set of sentences in L(G).

claim: Recursive descent uses mutually recursive procedures, one for each grammar nonterminal.
quote: A recursive-descent parser is structured as a set of mutually recursive procedures, one for each nonterminal in the grammar. The procedure that corresponds to nonterminal A recognizes an instance of A in the input stream.

claim: C's left-recursive additive productions have multiplicative expressions as operands, giving multiplication higher precedence and subtraction left associativity.
quote:
additive-expression:
multiplicative-expression
additive-expression + multiplicative-expression
additive-expression - multiplicative-expression

claim: The third edition calls the production-choice sets START sets and compares lookahead with them.
quote: Fig. 3.9 shows the START sets for the right-recursive expression grammar. A top-down parser can use START sets to pick the correct expansion for any nonterminal A by comparing the lookahead symbol to the START sets of the alternative right-hand sides for A.

claim: Crockford expands nud as null denotation and led as left denotation in an expression parser using binding powers.
quote: The technique we will develop here uses token objects whose members include binding powers (or precedence levels), and simple methods called nud (null denotation) and led (left denotation).

claim: An LR(1) parser generator allows either left or right recursion.
quote: With an LR(1) parser generator, the compiler writer can choose either left or right recursion to suit the circumstances.

claim: Bison supports left-recursive sequences and recommends them for bounded stack space.
quote: Any kind of sequence can be defined using either left recursion or right recursion, but you should always use left recursion, because it can parse a sequence of any number of elements with bounded stack space.

locator: The Bison Parser Algorithm, final two paragraphs before Look-Ahead Tokens
claim: Bison's shift/reduce parser is a bottom-up parser.
quote:
The parser tries, by shifts and reductions, to reduce the entire input down to a single grouping whose symbol is the grammar's start-symbol (see section Languages and Context-Free Grammars).

This kind of parser is known in the literature as a bottom-up parser.

claim: Parser error recovery allows continued parsing to find more syntax errors in one compilation.
quote: A parser should find as many syntax errors as possible in each compilation. The parser needs a mechanism that lets it “recover” from an error—that is, move to a state where it can continue parsing.
